topics.title: Micro vs macro: thinking in aggregates

learn.hook: One farmer in Punjab worries about the price of his wheat. The Finance Minister worries about the price of EVERYTHING at once. Welcome to macroeconomics!
points: Microeconomics studies individual units: one consumer, one firm, the market for one good like onions or cars.
Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole through aggregates: total output (GDP), total employment, the general price level, total saving and investment.

To keep things simple, macroeconomists often imagine all output as one representative good, so millions of separate markets are treated together (aggregate analysis instead of disaggregated analysis).
Economic agents are individuals or institutions that take economic decisions: households, firms, the government, and bodies like the RBI and SEBI.
Macroeconomic policy goals include higher growth, more employment, stable prices and better education and health for people.

example.q: Classify: (i) the price of tomatoes in Nashik; (ii) India's inflation rate; (iii) a firm's demand for steel; (iv) total employment in India.
steps: Ask: is it about one unit/market or the whole economy?
(i) one good's market → micro; (iii) one firm → micro
(ii) the general price level → macro; (iv) employment in the whole economy → macro
example.answer: (i) and (iii) are micro; (ii) and (iv) are macro

learn.reallife: When the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meets, it looks at aggregate inflation and GDP growth for all of India, not the price of one brand of biscuits.

quiz.explain: It examines individual markets (petrol and scooters), so it is a micro study.

options: Because individual data are always wrong

quiz.explain: Aggregates show the overall picture (growth, inflation, jobs) that policy-makers need.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My uncle studies the price of seeds. My aunt studies India's GDP. Aren't they both just doing economics?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Uncle studies one market (micro) and aunt studies aggregates for the whole economy (macro). Both are economics, at different levels!
teach.nudge: You've told me what uncle does. What makes aunt's work different? Think about the whole economy.

topics.title: Classical economics and the Great Depression

learn.hook: In 1929 the world's richest economy hit a wall: by 1933 one in every four American workers who wanted a job could not find one.
points: Adam Smith, author of 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776), is regarded as the founder of modern economics. Classical economists who followed him believed in free markets.
Classical view: if markets are left free, wages and prices adjust so that all who want work at the going wage find it; the economy tends to full employment by itself.
The Great Depression began in 1929. In the USA, output of goods and services fell sharply and the unemployment rate rose from about 3% to about 25% by 1933.
Unemployment rate = (number of people looking for work but jobless ÷ labour force) × 100, where the labour force = people working + people seeking work.
The long, deep slump showed that markets did not quickly correct themselves, which challenged the classical belief.

example.q: In a town, 1,840 people have jobs and 160 people are actively looking for work but jobless. Find the unemployment rate.

learn.reallife: During the COVID-19 lockdown in 2020, India's unemployment rate jumped sharply, reminding economists why the Great Depression made macroeconomics necessary.

topics.title: Keynes and the capitalist economy

learn.hook: One book in 1936 split economics into two branches. Its author, John Maynard Keynes, also helped design the post-war world money system at Bretton Woods.
points: John Maynard Keynes, a British economist, published 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' in 1936.
Keynes argued that output and employment depend on aggregate (effective) demand, and that an economy can stay stuck with unemployment for a long time.
His approach studied the economy as a whole, so 1936 is taken as the birth of macroeconomics as a separate branch.
A capitalist economy has: (a) private ownership of the means of production, (b) production mainly for sale in the market, and (c) sale and purchase of labour services at a wage rate.
In a capitalist economy, firms run by capitalists hire wage workers and produce goods for profit.

example.q: A village has a potter who makes pots only for his own family and a factory owner in Morbi who hires 200 workers on wages to make tiles for sale. Which shows capitalist production?
steps: Check the three features: private ownership, production for market sale, wage labour
The potter: no market sale, no hired labour
The Morbi factory: private owner, tiles sold, workers paid wages

learn.reallife: Modern India is a mixed economy, but large parts of it, such as private IT firms in Bengaluru hiring engineers for a salary to sell services worldwide, work on capitalist lines.

topics.title: Factors of production and the entrepreneur

learn.hook: Every rupee of income in India ends up in one of four pockets: rent, wages, interest or profit. Which pocket is yours?
points: Four factors of production: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
Their rewards (factor payments): land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest, entrepreneurship earns profit.
The entrepreneur organises the other factors, takes decisions and bears the risk of loss; profit is the reward for this risk-taking.
Investment expenditure is spending by firms on new machines, buildings and stocks; it adds to the productive capacity of the economy.

example.q: Raghav runs a dhaba on a highway. He rents the plot for ₹20,000 a month, pays cooks ₹45,000, pays ₹5,000 interest on a bank loan, and keeps what is left. Name each factor payment.
steps: Raghav (entrepreneur, bears the risk) → the remainder is profit
example.answer: Rent, wages, interest and profit respectively

learn.reallife: Startup founders in Bengaluru are entrepreneurs: they combine venture capital, rented office space and hired coders, and they earn profit only if the risk pays off.

topics.title: Four sectors of the macroeconomy

learn.hook: Your chai purchase, a GST payment and an Infosys export bill to the USA all belong to different 'sectors' of the same economy.
points: Macroeconomics groups economic agents into four sectors: households, firms, government and the external sector (rest of the world).
Households supply factor services (labour, land, capital) and buy consumer goods; firms hire factors and produce goods and services.
Government makes laws, enforces contracts, taxes people and firms, spends on public services and infrastructure, and regulates economic activity.
External sector: exports (goods sold abroad), imports (goods bought from abroad) and capital flows (foreign investment and borrowing).
A closed economy has no external sector; an open economy trades and has capital flows with other countries.

example.q: Assign each transaction to its sector: (i) Tata Motors hires workers; (ii) a family buys a fridge; (iii) the Centre collects income tax; (iv) India imports crude oil.
steps: (i) a producing unit hiring factors → firms
(iv) trade with other countries → external sector

learn.reallife: Remittances from Indians working in the Gulf and software exports to the USA connect India's households and firms with the external sector every day.

topics.title: Final, intermediate, consumption and capital goods

learn.hook: Milk poured on your cornflakes is a final good. The same milk poured into a chaiwala's kettle is an intermediate good. Same milk, different destiny!
points: Final goods are goods meant for final use (consumption or investment); they will not pass through any further stage of production in that year.
Intermediate goods are used up as inputs in producing other goods during the year, e.g. cotton bought by a textile mill.
Whether a good is final or intermediate depends on its use, not on what it is. Only final goods are counted in national income, to avoid double counting.
Consumption goods satisfy wants directly (food, clothes, haircuts). Consumer durables such as TVs, cars and fridges are consumption goods that last for years.
Capital goods (machines, tools, buildings) are durable goods used again and again in production; they are final goods but are not used up in one round.

example.q: Classify: (i) wheat bought by a flour mill; (ii) a tractor bought by a farmer; (iii) a washing machine bought by a family; (iv) paper bought by a publisher.
steps: (i) wheat is used up to make flour → intermediate
(ii) the tractor is used again and again to produce crops → capital good (final)
(iii) used by a household for years → consumer durable (final)
(iv) paper becomes part of books → intermediate
example.answer: (i) intermediate, (ii) capital good, (iii) consumer durable, (iv) intermediate

learn.reallife: Steel sold by SAIL to Maruti Suzuki is intermediate, but the Swift car bought by a family is a final consumer durable. NSO counts only the car's value to avoid counting the steel twice.

topics.title: Stocks, flows, investment and depreciation

learn.hook: A water tank at a given moment holds 500 litres: that's a stock. Water flowing in at 10 litres a minute: that's a flow. The economy works the same way.
points: A stock is measured at a point of time (wealth, capital, money supply on 31 March). A flow is measured over a period of time (income, output, investment per year).
Water-tank analogy: the water in the tank is a stock; water entering per minute is a flow. Capital is a stock; investment is the flow that adds to it.
Gross investment = total addition to capital goods (and inventories) in a year.
Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital) = fall in the value of fixed capital due to normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence.
Net investment = Gross investment − Depreciation. Only net investment adds to the capital stock.

example.q: A firm buys a machine for ₹10,00,000 that lasts 20 years with no scrap value. In a year it also spends ₹2,00,000 on new equipment. Find annual depreciation of the first machine and the year's net investment, if the 2,00,000 is the year's gross investment.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways adds new Vande Bharat trainsets (gross investment) while old coaches wear out (depreciation). Its fleet grows only by the difference.

topics.title: Circular flow of income

learn.hook: Every rupee a firm pays as wages comes back to it when workers shop. Money in an economy runs in a circle, like a lap around the Eden Gardens boundary.
points: Two-sector model: only households and firms. Households supply factor services; firms supply goods and services. This is the real flow.
The money flow runs the other way: firms pay factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) to households; households spend this money on firms' goods.
Simplifying assumptions: no government, no foreign trade, and households spend all their income (no saving), so there are no leakages.
Under these assumptions, aggregate output = aggregate factor income = aggregate expenditure. Each is a measurement point for national income.
This gives the three methods of measuring national income: product (value added), income and expenditure methods.

example.q: In a two-sector economy with no saving, firms produce goods worth ₹500 crore. What are the aggregate factor incomes and aggregate expenditure?
steps: The whole value of output is paid as factor incomes → ₹500 crore
With no saving, households spend all income on firms' output → ₹500 crore

learn.reallife: When a Swiggy delivery partner earns wages and spends them at a kirana store, money moves from firm to household and back to a firm: the circular flow in action.

games.title: Follow the rupee
games.prompt: Arrange one round of the money flow
items: Firms pay wages, rent, interest and profit to households
Households spend their income on goods and services
Firms receive sales revenue and pay factors again

games.title: Circular flow facts
items: In the two-sector model there is no government.
Only households and firms are present.
Factor services flow from firms to households.
Households supply factor services to firms.
Money flow and real flow move in opposite directions.
Goods go to households while money goes to firms, and so on.
In the simple model households save a part of their income.
It assumes no saving, so there is no leakage.
Aggregate output equals aggregate factor income in the simple model.
All value produced is paid out as factor incomes.

options: Goods and services and factor payments
quiz.explain: Households provide factor services (real flow) and spend money on goods (money flow) to firms.

quiz.explain: No saving, no government and no foreign trade means no leakages.

quiz.explain: Payments of wages, rent, interest and profit are money flows.

options: the government forces them to be equal

quiz.explain: Revenue received by firms from sales is distributed as rewards to the factors that produced the goods.

options: Labour services supplied by households to firms

quiz.mistake: Treats money payments as real flows

quiz.explain: In the simple model, output = income = expenditure, so factor income is ₹1,200 crore.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In the simplest two-sector model, there are no leakages from the circular flow. Reason (R): The model assumes no saving, no taxes and no imports.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: Saving, taxes and imports are the leakages, and all are assumed away.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise saving, taxes and imports as leakages

options: production, income and expenditure points of the circular flow
quiz.explain: National income can be measured at the production point, the income point or the expenditure point.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up methods with unrelated concepts

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Where does the money go after I pay the baker? Does it just vanish?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Your money goes to the firm, which pays it as factor income to households, who spend it again. It flows in a circle!
teach.nudge: You said the baker gets the money. What does the baker's firm do with it next?

topics.title: Product method: value added

learn.hook: If you add the value of wheat, flour and bread, you count the wheat three times. Value added fixes this classic trap.
points: Value added (gross) = value of output − intermediate consumption (inputs bought from other firms).
Farmer-baker idea: if a farmer grows wheat with no inputs and sells part to a baker who makes bread, adding both outputs counts the wheat twice; adding value added counts it once.
Gross value added (GVA) − depreciation = net value added (NVA).
GDP = sum of the gross value added of all producing units in the domestic territory.
Value added by a firm is the reward available for its factors of production (wages, rent, interest, profit).

example.q: A farmer grows cotton worth ₹50 (no inputs) and sells it all to a weaver. The weaver makes cloth worth ₹120 and sells it to a tailor, who makes shirts worth ₹200. Find total value added and show the double counting.
steps: Total value added = 50 + 70 + 80 = 200 (equals the final good's value)
example.answer: Value added = ₹200; summing outputs (₹370) double counts

learn.reallife: Amul's value added is the value of its butter, cheese and milk powder minus the milk and packaging it buys; adding up such value added across all Indian producers gives GDP.

items.text: Value added = value of output − ___ consumption.
NVA = GVA − ___.
GDP is the sum of ___ value added of all producing units.
Adding the values of all goods at every stage leads to ___ counting.

quiz.q: A firm's value of output is ₹800 and it buys raw materials worth ₹350. What is its gross value added (in ₹)?
quiz.explain: GVA = value of output − intermediate consumption = 800 − 350 = 450.
quiz.mistake: Adds inputs to output instead of subtracting

quiz.q: A farmer grows wheat worth ₹100 without buying inputs and sells it to a baker, who makes bread worth ₹250. The GDP contribution of the two is (₹)
quiz.explain: Value added: farmer 100, baker 250 − 100 = 150; total = 250, equal to the final good (bread).
quiz.mistake: Adds both outputs and double counts the wheat

quiz.q: Gross value added of a firm is ₹600 and depreciation is ₹45. Net value added (₹) is
quiz.explain: NVA = GVA − depreciation = 600 − 45 = 555.

quiz.q: GDP by the product method is the sum of
options: gross value added of all producing units
value of output of all firms
net value added of all firms
sales of final goods minus exports
quiz.explain: GDP adds up GVA across all firms; summing outputs double counts.
quiz.mistake: Adds total output, causing double counting

quiz.q: Which item is deducted from the value of output to find a firm's value added?
options: Raw materials bought from other firms
quiz.explain: Intermediate inputs are deducted. Wages, interest and profit are paid out of value added.
quiz.mistake: Deducts factor payments, which are part of value added

quiz.q: Three firms have outputs of ₹100 (no inputs), ₹180 (inputs ₹100) and ₹300 (inputs ₹180). Total value added (₹) is
quiz.explain: Value added = 100 + 80 + 120 = 300, equal to the value of the final output.
quiz.mistake: Adds outputs (580) rather than value added

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Adding the value of output of all firms overstates GDP. Reason (R): The value of intermediate goods gets counted more than once.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Intermediate inputs are included in each buyer's output again, which is double counting.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why summing outputs inflates GDP

quiz.q: Value added by a firm is distributed as
options: wages, rent, interest and profit to factors
quiz.explain: Value added is the income created by the firm, paid to its factors of production.
quiz.mistake: Thinks value added pays for inputs

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'To find India's GDP, can't I just add up the sales of every company?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Adding sales would count inputs again and again. Add each firm's value added (output minus intermediate inputs) instead!
teach.nudge: Close! What goes wrong if we add the wheat, the flour and the bread? How do we fix it?

topics.title: Inventories: planned and unplanned

learn.hook: A Diwali sweet shop makes 500 kg of kaju katli but sells only 450 kg. The extra 50 kg is still part of what it produced this year.
points: Inventory (stock) = unsold finished goods, semi-finished goods and raw materials a firm carries from one year to the next.
Value of output = value of sales + change in inventories (stock).
Change in inventories during a year = closing stock − opening stock = production − sales. It can be positive (accumulation) or negative (decumulation).
Change in inventories is treated as investment, because it adds to the firm's stock of goods.
Planned inventory change is what the firm intended; unplanned change happens when sales differ from expectations (e.g. sales fall short → unplanned accumulation).

example.q: A firm's sales in a year are ₹5,000. Its opening stock is ₹400 and closing stock ₹650. Find the change in stock and the value of output.
steps: Value of output = sales + change in stock
example.answer: Change in stock ₹250; value of output ₹5,250

learn.reallife: Car makers in India often see unplanned inventory pile up at dealers when festive-season sales are weaker than expected.

items.q: Opening stock 30, closing stock 80. Change in stock?

games.title: Planned or unplanned?
items: A firm deliberately builds up stock before Diwali
Sales fall short of forecast, so stock piles up
A firm decides to keep a bigger raw-material buffer
A sudden rush of buyers empties the warehouse
A shop plans to clear old stock in a sale and does so
Exports get cancelled and goods stay unsold

quiz.q: Sales of a firm are ₹2,000 and change in stock is ₹150. The value of output (₹) is
quiz.explain: Value of output = sales + change in stock = 2,000 + 150 = 2,150.

quiz.q: A firm's opening stock is ₹600 and closing stock ₹450. Its sales are ₹3,000. Value of output (₹) is
quiz.mistake: Uses opening − closing, getting the sign of the change wrong

quiz.q: Change in inventories is included in national income accounts as part of

quiz.mistake: Thinks unsold goods are not counted at all

quiz.q: A firm expected to sell goods worth ₹1,000 but sold only ₹900, having produced ₹1,000. The unplanned inventory change (₹) is
quiz.explain: Unsold goods of ₹100 piled up unexpectedly: an unplanned accumulation of +100.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign wrong; an excess of output over sales adds to stock

quiz.q: Unplanned decumulation of inventories happens when
options: sales turn out lower than expected
sales turn out higher than expected
quiz.explain: If buyers buy more than expected, stocks fall below plan.

quiz.q: Production of a firm is ₹700 and its sales are ₹760. The change in inventories (₹) is
quiz.explain: Change in inventories = production − sales = 700 − 760 = −60 (stocks fell).
quiz.mistake: Takes sales − production, flipping the sign

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Inventory is a stock while change in inventory is a flow. Reason (R): Change in inventory is measured over a period of time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Inventory is measured at a point of time; its change over the year is a flow.
quiz.mistake: Thinks inventory and its change are the same type of variable

quiz.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Value of output = sales + change in stock
Value of output = sales − closing stock
Value of output = closing stock − sales
quiz.explain: Goods produced but not sold are still output, so the change in stock is added to sales.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If a shop makes 100 laddoos and sells only 80, did it produce 80 or 100?'
teach.praise: Chirp! It produced 100: sales of 80 plus a change in stock of 20. Unsold laddoos still count as output!
teach.nudge: Hmm, what about the 20 unsold laddoos? Do they count as production?

topics.title: Expenditure and income methods

learn.hook: You can count India's GDP three ways and should get the same answer every time, like checking a sum by adding columns and then rows.
points: Expenditure method: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M), where C = private final consumption, I = investment (including inventory change), G = government final consumption, X − M = net exports.
Imports are subtracted because C, I and G include spending on foreign goods that were not produced at home.

Income method: GDP = W + P + In + R in the simple model (wages, profits, interest, rent). In Indian accounts the components are compensation of employees, operating surplus (rent, interest, profit) and mixed income of the self-employed.
Strictly, adding factor incomes gives domestic income (NDP at factor cost); adding depreciation and net indirect taxes takes it to GDP at market prices.
Product, income and expenditure methods give the same GDP, because output = income = expenditure.

example.q: C = 600, I = 200, G = 150, X = 80, M = 110 (₹ crore). Find GDP by the expenditure method.

learn.reallife: India imports most of its crude oil; when petrol prices rise, spending on imports grows, which lowers net exports (X − M) in the GDP calculation.

items.q: Wages 400, rent 50, interest 30, profit 120. Total factor income?
Compensation 700, operating surplus 250, mixed income 50. Total?
GDP 1000, C 600, I 200, G 150. Net exports?

quiz.q: GDP by the expenditure method equals
quiz.explain: Final expenditure on domestic output = consumption + investment + government spending + net exports.
quiz.mistake: Adds imports instead of subtracting them

quiz.q: Private consumption 1,200, investment 400, government consumption 300, exports 200, imports 250 (₹ crore). GDP (₹ crore) is
Why are imports subtracted in the expenditure method?
options: Spending on imports buys goods produced abroad, not domestic output
Imports are a form of saving
quiz.explain: C, I and G include spending on foreign goods; subtracting M leaves only spending on domestic production.
quiz.mistake: Thinks imports are deducted for policy reasons

quiz.q: Compensation of employees ₹500 crore, rent ₹60 crore, interest ₹40 crore, profit ₹200 crore, mixed income ₹100 crore. Domestic factor income (₹ crore) is
quiz.mistake: Leaves out mixed income or one component of operating surplus

quiz.q: Operating surplus is the sum of
quiz.explain: Operating surplus = rent + interest + profit; compensation of employees is separate.

quiz.q: The income of a self-employed tailor who uses her own shop and machine is recorded as
quiz.explain: Self-employed people earn a mix of wages, rent, interest and profit that cannot be separated, called mixed income.
quiz.mistake: Treats self-employed income as a salary

quiz.q: Assertion (A): GDP measured by the product, income and expenditure methods is the same. Reason (R): Value of output is fully paid out as factor incomes and is fully bought as final expenditure.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Because output = income = expenditure in the circular flow, the three methods agree.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the three methods measure different things

quiz.q: In an economy GDP is ₹2,000 crore, C = 1,300, I = 400 and G = 250 (₹ crore). Net exports (₹ crore) are
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign slip while rearranging

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Can you measure India's GDP by looking at spending or at incomes? Won't they disagree?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Spending (C + I + G + X − M) and incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) both give the same GDP. Two roads, one destination!
teach.nudge: You explained one method. What is the other, and do they give the same number?

topics.title: Factor cost, basic prices and market prices

learn.hook: A packet of biscuits costs ₹30 in the shop, but the factors who made it earned less than that. The gap is mostly GST, a product tax.
points: Market price = what buyers pay. Factor cost = what the factors of production receive.
GDP at market prices − net indirect taxes = GDP at factor cost, where net indirect taxes = indirect taxes − subsidies.

Production taxes and subsidies are linked to production but not to the quantity produced (land revenue, stamp and registration fees, professional tax). Product taxes and subsidies are levied per unit of product (GST, excise duty, customs duty).
GVA at basic prices = GVA at factor cost + (production taxes − production subsidies). GVA at market prices = GVA at basic prices + (product taxes − product subsidies).
India's national accounts (NSO) report sector-wise GVA at basic prices, and GDP at market prices for the whole economy.

example.q: GDP at market prices is ₹5,000 crore, indirect taxes are ₹600 crore and subsidies ₹100 crore. Find GDP at factor cost.
steps: GDP at FC = GDP at MP − NIT

learn.reallife: When the government cuts fertiliser prices through subsidies, the market price farmers pay falls below factor cost, so subsidies are added back when moving from market price to factor cost.

items.q: GVA FC 400, production taxes 30, production subsidies 10. GVA basic?
GVA basic 420, product taxes 60, product subsidies 20. GVA MP?
GDP MP 1000, indirect taxes 90, subsidies 40. GDP FC?

quiz.q: GDP at market prices is ₹8,000 crore, indirect taxes ₹900 crore and subsidies ₹200 crore. GDP at factor cost (₹ crore) is
quiz.explain: GDP at FC = GDP at MP − (indirect taxes − subsidies) = 8,000 − 700 = 7,300.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts subsidies too instead of adding them back

quiz.q: Which of these is a product tax?
quiz.explain: GST is levied per unit of the product sold; the others are production taxes not tied to quantity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every indirect tax is a product tax

quiz.q: GVA at basic prices equals
options: GVA at factor cost + product taxes − product subsidies
GVA at market prices + production taxes
GVA at factor cost + production taxes − production subsidies
quiz.explain: Basic prices add net production taxes to factor cost; product taxes come in only at market prices.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up production and product taxes

quiz.q: GVA at basic prices is ₹2,000 crore, product taxes are ₹300 crore and product subsidies ₹50 crore. GVA at market prices (₹ crore) is
quiz.mistake: Adds subsidies instead of subtracting them

quiz.q: Subsidies are added when moving from GDP at market prices to GDP at factor cost because
options: subsidies make market prices lower than what factors receive
quiz.explain: With a subsidy, buyers pay less than factor cost, so it must be added back.

quiz.q: In India's national accounts, industry-wise output is reported as
quiz.explain: NSO reports sector-wise GVA at basic prices and GDP at market prices.

quiz.q: GDP at factor cost is ₹4,200 crore and net indirect taxes are ₹350 crore. GDP at market prices (₹ crore) is
quiz.explain: GDP at MP = GDP at FC + NIT = 4,200 + 350 = 4,550.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts NIT when going from FC to MP

quiz.q: Assertion (A): GDP at market prices is usually greater than GDP at factor cost. Reason (R): Indirect taxes usually exceed subsidies.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: When net indirect taxes are positive, market price value exceeds factor cost value.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the gap to net indirect taxes

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does India's GDP have so many prices—market, basic and factor cost?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Factor cost is what producers' factors earn; add net production taxes for basic prices and net product taxes for market prices!
teach.nudge: You said taxes matter. What about subsidies? Which way do they move the price?

topics.title: GNP, NNP and national income

learn.hook: An Indian engineer working in Dubai adds to India's national income but not to India's domestic product. Domestic and national are not the same!
points: Domestic = produced within the country's territory. National = earned by the country's normal residents, wherever they work.
NFIA (net factor income from abroad) = factor income earned by residents from abroad − factor income earned by non-residents in the domestic territory.
GNP = GDP + NFIA. NDP = GDP − depreciation. NNP = GNP − depreciation.
National income (NI) = NNP at factor cost = NNP at market prices − net indirect taxes = NDP at factor cost + NFIA.
If NFIA is negative (as for India in recent years, due to large interest and profit payments abroad), GNP is less than GDP.

example.q: GDP at market prices = 2,500, NFIA = −50, net indirect taxes = 200, national income = 2,000 (₹ crore). Find depreciation.
steps: NNP at FC = GNP at MP − depreciation − NIT

learn.reallife: Profits sent home by foreign companies operating in India are a factor income paid abroad, which is one reason India's NFIA is negative.

items.q: Income from abroad 30, paid abroad 45. NFIA?

quiz.q: Net factor income from abroad is defined as
options: factor income earned by residents abroad minus factor income earned by non-residents in the domestic territory
foreign aid received minus aid given
quiz.explain: NFIA is about factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit), not trade in goods.

quiz.q: GDP at market prices is ₹10,000 crore and NFIA is −₹200 crore. GNP at market prices (₹ crore) is
quiz.mistake: Ignores the negative sign of NFIA

quiz.q: NNP at market prices is ₹6,500 crore, indirect taxes ₹700 crore and subsidies ₹150 crore. National income (₹ crore) is
quiz.mistake: Subtracts both indirect taxes and subsidies

quiz.q: NDP at factor cost is ₹3,000 crore and NFIA is ₹40 crore. National income (₹ crore) is
quiz.explain: NI = NDP at FC + NFIA = 3,000 + 40 = 3,040.

quiz.q: GDP at market prices = ₹1,800 crore, NFIA = ₹20 crore, net indirect taxes = ₹150 crore, national income = ₹1,500 crore. Depreciation (₹ crore) is
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add NFIA before working back

quiz.q: When will GNP be less than GDP?
options: When net factor income from abroad is negative
quiz.explain: GNP = GDP + NFIA, so a negative NFIA makes GNP smaller.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up NFIA with net exports or depreciation

quiz.q: Wages earned by an Indian resident working temporarily at a US embassy in New Delhi are
options: part of India's national income but not its domestic product
quiz.explain: Embassies are not part of the domestic territory of the host country, so the income is earned outside India's domestic territory by an Indian resident: it is factor income from abroad.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything in New Delhi is domestic territory

quiz.q: Assertion (A): National income can be greater than domestic income. Reason (R): NFIA can be positive.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: NI = domestic income (NDP FC) + NFIA, so a positive NFIA makes national income larger.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect NFIA to the domestic–national gap

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is the difference between GDP and GNP, and how do I reach national income?'
teach.praise: Tweet! GNP adds NFIA to GDP; subtract depreciation for NNP and net indirect taxes for national income (NNP at factor cost)!
teach.nudge: You started with GDP. What do we add to get GNP, and what do we take away to reach national income?

topics.title: Personal income, disposable income and the saving gap

learn.hook: National income is what the nation earns, but not all of it reaches your family's wallet. Companies keep some, the taxman takes some, and pensions add some back.
points: Personal income (PI) = NI − undistributed profits − net interest payments made by households − corporate tax + transfer payments to households (from government and firms).
Personal disposable income (PDI) = PI − personal tax payments − non-tax payments (such as fines). Households either consume or save PDI.
National disposable income = NNP at market prices + other current transfers from the rest of the world (gifts, aid, remittances).
Private income = factor income from NDP accruing to the private sector + national debt interest + NFIA + current transfers from government + other net transfers from the rest of the world.
From Y = C + I + G + X − M and Y = C + S + T: (S − I) = (G − T) + (X − M). Excess private saving over investment finances the budget deficit plus the trade surplus.

example.q: NI = 5,000, undistributed profits = 300, net interest paid by households = 100, corporate tax = 400, transfers to households = 250, personal taxes = 500, non-tax payments = 50 (₹ crore). Find PI and PDI.
steps: PDI = PI − personal taxes − non-tax payments

learn.reallife: PM-KISAN payments to farmers and old-age pensions are transfers: they raise personal income without being payment for current production.

games.title: Add or subtract when going from NI to PI?

items.text: PDI = PI − personal taxes − ___ payments.
National disposable income = NNP at market prices + other current ___ from the rest of the world.
Profits kept by companies and not paid as dividends are called ___ profits.

quiz.q: NI ₹8,000 crore, undistributed profits ₹500 crore, corporate tax ₹700 crore, net interest paid by households ₹200 crore, transfers to households ₹400 crore. Personal income (₹ crore) is
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the transfers instead of adding them

quiz.q: Personal income is ₹3,600 crore, personal taxes ₹450 crore and fines and fees ₹30 crore. PDI (₹ crore) is
Which item is ADDED to national income to get personal income?
quiz.explain: Transfers reach households without current production, so they are added; the others are subtracted.

quiz.q: National disposable income is NNP at market prices plus
options: other current transfers from the rest of the world
quiz.explain: It shows the total goods and services a nation can use from its income and receipts from abroad.
quiz.mistake: Adds depreciation and confuses it with GNP

quiz.q: Which is included in private income but NOT in national income?
options: Wages earned in the private sector
quiz.explain: National debt interest is a transfer (the debt mostly financed non-productive needs), so it enters private income but not NI.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all interest is factor income

quiz.q: Private saving is ₹500 crore, investment ₹400 crore and the budget deficit (G − T) is ₹150 crore. Using (S − I) = (G − T) + (X − M), net exports (₹ crore) are
quiz.explain: S − I = 100 = 150 + (X − M), so X − M = −50: a trade deficit of 50.

quiz.q: Private saving exceeds investment by ₹80 crore and the trade surplus (X − M) is ₹30 crore. The budget deficit (₹ crore) is
quiz.mistake: Adds the trade surplus instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Personal disposable income is smaller than personal income. Reason (R): Households must pay personal taxes and non-tax payments such as fines out of personal income.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: PDI = PI − personal taxes − non-tax payments, so it is smaller whenever these are positive.
quiz.mistake: Does not see what is deducted to reach PDI

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'India earns a huge national income, so why does my family get much less to spend?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Firms keep undistributed profits and pay corporate tax, transfers are added, and personal taxes go out before we get disposable income!
teach.nudge: You've named the taxes. What gets added back to households, like pensions?

topics.title: Nominal GDP, real GDP and the GDP deflator

learn.hook: If India's GDP doubles because every price doubled, are we any richer? Real GDP answers that by freezing prices.
points: Nominal GDP values each year's output at that year's (current) prices.
Real GDP values each year's output at the prices of a fixed base year (constant prices), so it changes only when quantities change.
GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100. NCERT also writes it as the ratio itself (e.g. 1.2 instead of 120).
In the base year, nominal GDP = real GDP and the deflator is 100. A deflator above 100 means prices have risen since the base year.
Real GDP = Nominal GDP ÷ (deflator ÷ 100).

topics.title: CPI, WPI and the deflator compared

learn.hook: When your family's grocery bill jumps, that is CPI talking. When a factory's raw-material bill jumps, that is WPI.
points: Consumer Price Index (CPI) = (cost of a fixed basket of consumer goods at current prices ÷ its cost at base-year prices) × 100.
Wholesale Price Index (WPI) measures changes in prices of goods traded in bulk at the wholesale level; in many countries it is called the Producer Price Index (PPI).
Difference 1 (coverage): CPI covers goods bought by consumers; the GDP deflator covers all final goods and services produced in the economy.
Difference 2 (imports): CPI includes prices of imported consumer goods; the GDP deflator does not, since it covers only domestic output.
Difference 3 (weights): CPI uses fixed base-year quantities (weights); the deflator's weights change each year with the actual production.

example.q: A basket of 10 kg rice and 5 kg dal cost ₹300 in the base year. Now rice is ₹40/kg and dal ₹100/kg. Find CPI.
steps: Current cost of the same basket = 10 × 40 + 5 × 100 = 400 + 500 = 900

topics.title: GDP and welfare

learn.hook: A city can post record GDP while its air becomes unbreathable. Is everyone really better off?
points: Higher GDP does not always mean higher welfare (well-being) of people; GDP is an incomplete index of welfare.
Distribution: if GDP rises but the increase goes to a few rich people, most people may be no better off or even worse off.
Non-monetary exchanges: housework, help within families and barter are not counted in GDP, so GDP understates real activity.
Externalities: benefits or harms to others that are not paid for. Pollution by a factory is a negative externality not deducted from GDP; a well-kept garden that neighbours enjoy is a positive one.
So per capita real GDP must be read alongside distribution, environment and non-market work when judging welfare.

example.q: Village A's income rose from ₹100 lakh to ₹120 lakh, but the whole rise went to one landowner while 90% of families' incomes fell. Did welfare rise?
steps: But the gain went to one person and most families became poorer
example.answer: Not necessarily: most people are worse off despite higher GDP

learn.reallife: Delhi's winter smog shows a negative externality: vehicle and crop-burning pollution harms health, yet the harm is not subtracted from GDP.

topics.title: From barter to money

learn.hook: Imagine paying for a movie ticket with two coconuts and a pencil, and the ticket seller wants rice. That is barter, and its headaches are why money was invented.
points: Barter = direct exchange of goods for goods (commodity for commodity) without money.

Drawbacks of barter: (1) need for a double coincidence of wants; (2) no common measure of value; (3) indivisibility of some goods (you cannot split a cow); (4) difficulty in storing wealth, since many goods perish or lose value.
Money is anything commonly accepted as a medium of exchange and a means of payment.
Medium of exchange: money separates buying from selling, removing the need for double coincidence of wants.
Unit of account (measure of value): values of all goods are expressed in money (₹), so relative prices are easy to compare. If a pen costs ₹20 and a notebook ₹60, one notebook = 3 pens.

example.q: A farmer with wheat wants shoes, but the cobbler wants milk, not wheat. Explain the problem and how money solves it.
steps: The farmer's want (shoes) and the cobbler's want (milk) do not match
This is the lack of double coincidence of wants
With money, the farmer sells wheat to anyone for ₹ and pays the cobbler in ₹
example.answer: Money as a medium of exchange removes the need for double coincidence of wants

learn.reallife: When you scan a UPI QR code at a tea stall, rupees act as the medium of exchange and the menu prices (₹15 a cup) act as the unit of account.

topics.title: Store of value, purchasing power and digital money

learn.hook: ₹1,000 under your pillow keeps its number but not its power. If prices double, it buys only half as much.
points: Store of value: money lets people store wealth and spend it later. Money is the most liquid asset: it can be used for payment instantly without loss.
Other assets (land, gold, bonds, houses) may earn returns but are less liquid; converting them to money takes time and cost.
Purchasing power of money is the amount of goods one unit of money can buy. It falls when the general price level rises (purchasing power ∝ 1/price level).
Digital and cashless payments: Jan Dhan bank accounts, Aadhaar-enabled payment systems, e-wallets, UPI and the National Financial Switch (the network linking ATMs of different banks).

Demonetisation (8 November 2016): old ₹500 and ₹1000 notes ceased to be legal tender; aims included curbing black money, counterfeit notes and terror financing and promoting digital payments. New ₹500 and ₹2000 notes were issued.

example.q: Prices in the economy double. What happens to the purchasing power of ₹500?
steps: Purchasing power varies inversely with the price level
If the price level doubles, each rupee buys half as much

topics.title: Demand for money

learn.hook: Why keep cash in your wallet that earns nothing, when a fixed deposit pays interest? Because you need it to buy things, and sometimes to wait for a better chance.
points: Transaction demand: people hold money to make payments. It rises with income (more transactions) and is written M_T = kPY, where PY is nominal income and k is the fraction of income held as money.
k = 1/v, where v is the velocity of circulation (the number of times a unit of money changes hands in a year). If v = 4, k = 1/4.
Holding money has an opportunity cost: the interest given up. So a higher interest rate lowers the demand for money.
Speculative demand: bond prices and the interest rate move inversely. When the rate is high, people expect it to fall (bond prices to rise), so they buy bonds and hold less money.
Liquidity trap: at a very low interest rate everyone expects it to rise and bond prices to fall, so people hold any extra money and money demand becomes perfectly elastic.

example.q: Nominal income in an economy is ₹2,400 crore and the velocity of money is 6. Find the transaction demand for money.

learn.reallife: When FD rates rise, many Indian families shift money out of savings accounts into deposits, holding less idle money.

topics.title: Supply of money: M1 to M4

learn.hook: The rupee note in your pocket says 'I promise to pay the bearer...' and is signed by the RBI Governor. Yet it has almost no value as paper. So what makes it money?
points: Money supply is the total stock of money held by the public at a point of time. M1 = CU + DD (currency notes and coins held by the public + net demand deposits held by commercial banks).

M2 = M1 + savings deposits with Post Office savings banks. M3 = M1 + net time deposits of commercial banks. M4 = M3 + total deposits with Post Office savings organisations (excluding National Savings Certificates).
M1 and M2 are narrow money; M3 and M4 are broad money. Liquidity falls from M1 to M4. M3 is the most commonly used measure (aggregate monetary resources).
Currency notes are issued by the RBI; coins (and one-rupee notes) are issued by the Government of India. Currency is fiat money: it has no intrinsic value and is money by government order.
Currency is legal tender: it cannot be refused in settling payments. Cheques and demand deposits are not legal tender; a payee may refuse a cheque.

example.q: The public holds currency of ₹30 lakh crore; net demand deposits are ₹25 lakh crore; net time deposits of banks are ₹150 lakh crore. Find M1 and M3.

topics.title: The Reserve Bank of India and its functions

learn.hook: During the 2008 global crisis and again in 2020, when banks feared a cash crunch, one institution in Mumbai stood ready to lend: the RBI.
points: The Reserve Bank of India was set up in 1935 as India's central bank. It is the apex monetary authority.
Bank of issue (currency authority): it has the sole right to issue currency notes (other than one-rupee notes), backed by assets such as foreign securities and gold.
Banker to the government: keeps government accounts, makes payments and receives deposits for it, manages its borrowing and advises it on financial matters.
Banker's bank and supervisor: commercial banks keep reserves with it; it lends to them as the lender of last resort in a crisis, and it regulates and supervises banks.
Custodian of foreign exchange reserves and controller of credit: manages India's forex reserves and controls money supply and credit through monetary policy.

example.q: A bank faces a sudden rush of withdrawals and cannot borrow from other banks. Which RBI function helps, and how?
steps: The bank has no other source of funds
The RBI can lend to it when no one else will
This is the lender of last resort function
example.answer: Lender of last resort, part of the RBI's role as banker's bank

learn.reallife: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee announces the repo rate, while its banking supervision teams inspect banks like any regulator would.

topics.title: Commercial banks, balance sheets and the goldsmith's secret

learn.hook: Centuries ago a goldsmith noticed something clever: people who left gold with him rarely all came back for it on the same day.
points: Commercial banks accept deposits from the public and lend to households and firms. They earn the spread: the difference between the interest rate on loans and the rate paid on deposits.
A bank's balance sheet: assets (reserves with itself and with the RBI, loans given, investments) and liabilities (deposits of the public, borrowings). Net worth = assets − liabilities.

Goldsmith story: people deposited gold for safety and received receipts; the receipts began to circulate as money. Since only a fraction of gold was withdrawn at a time, the goldsmith lent out the rest and earned interest.
This is fractional reserve banking: banks keep only a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend the rest.
By lending and creating new demand deposits, commercial banks create money; deposits are part of money supply.

example.q: A bank pays 4% interest on deposits and charges 9% on loans. It has deposits of ₹10 crore and loans of ₹8 crore. Find its spread rate and simple annual interest margin (ignoring reserves' returns).
steps: Interest earned on loans = 9% of 8 = ₹0.72 crore
Interest paid on deposits = 4% of 10 = ₹0.40 crore

learn.reallife: When you deposit ₹10,000 in a savings account at a public sector bank, the bank keeps a part as reserves and lends much of the rest as home or business loans.

topics.title: Credit creation and the money multiplier

learn.hook: Deposit ₹1,000 in a bank, and with a 10% reserve ratio the banking system can turn it into ₹10,000 of deposits. Magic? No, arithmetic.
points: With reserve ratio r, a bank keeps r of each new deposit as reserves and lends the rest. The loan is spent and redeposited, and the process repeats round after round.
Money multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio. With r = 20%, the multiplier is 1/0.2 = 5.
Total deposits created = initial deposit × money multiplier. Credit (loans) created = total deposits − initial deposit, since the initial deposit itself is kept as reserves in the end.
High powered money (reserve money) H = currency held by the public + reserves of banks (vault cash and deposits with the RBI). Money supply = money multiplier × H.
Limits: the reserve requirement, and leakages such as people holding cash instead of redepositing. A higher reserve ratio lowers the multiplier and the money supply.

example.q: An initial deposit is ₹1,000 and the reserve ratio is 10%. Show the first two rounds and find total deposits and total credit created.

learn.reallife: When the RBI cuts the CRR, banks such as SBI and HDFC can lend more out of each deposit, which raises the money multiplier.

items.q: Multiplier 8. Reserve ratio as a fraction?

topics.title: Quantitative tools: CRR, SLR, repo and OMO

learn.hook: Every two months, crores of rupees of home and car loans become cheaper or costlier depending on one number the RBI announces: the repo rate.
points: Quantitative instruments affect the total volume of credit; qualitative (selective) instruments affect its direction and use.

Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR): the fraction of deposits banks must keep as cash reserves with the RBI. Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): the fraction of deposits banks must keep in liquid assets such as cash, gold and approved government securities.

Bank rate: the rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks. Repo rate: the rate at which the RBI lends short-term to banks against government securities, with an agreement to repurchase them. Reverse repo rate: the rate at which the RBI borrows from banks.
Open market operations (OMO): outright purchase or sale of government securities by the RBI in the market. RBI buying securities injects money; selling absorbs money.
Raising CRR, SLR, bank rate or repo rate, or selling securities, contracts credit; lowering them or buying securities expands credit.

example.q: To fight high inflation, what should the RBI do with (i) the repo rate and (ii) open market operations?
steps: Inflation is a case of excess demand, so credit must be reduced
(i) Raise the repo rate so borrowing becomes costlier
(ii) Sell government securities to absorb money from banks
example.answer: Raise the repo rate and sell government securities

learn.reallife: When the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee raises the repo rate, banks usually raise EMIs on loans linked to the repo rate.

topics.title: Qualitative tools, using the toolkit and sterilisation

learn.hook: Sometimes the RBI doesn't change any rate at all. It simply 'requests' banks to go slow on certain loans, and they listen.
points: Margin requirement: the part of a security's value that a borrower must pay from own funds (loan = value − margin). Raising the margin reduces the loan available against that security.
Moral suasion: persuasion, requests and advice by the RBI to banks to follow its policy, e.g. to restrict or expand credit to certain sectors.
Excess demand (inflation): raise repo rate, bank rate, CRR, SLR and margin requirements; sell securities; use moral suasion to restrict credit.
Deficient demand (recession): lower repo rate, bank rate, CRR, SLR and margins; buy securities; encourage banks to lend.

Sterilisation: when large foreign capital inflows raise money supply (because the RBI buys foreign exchange), the RBI sells government securities to absorb the extra money and protect the economy from inflation.

example.q: A borrower pledges shares worth ₹1,00,000 and the margin requirement is 40%. How much loan can he get? What happens if the margin rises to 60%?

learn.reallife: When foreign portfolio investors pour dollars into Indian markets, the RBI buys dollars to steady the rupee and may sterilise the extra rupees by selling bonds.

chapters.title: Macroeconomics: Determination of Income and Employment

topics.title: Ex ante, ex post and aggregate demand

learn.hook: A biscuit factory PLANS to add ₹10 lakh to its stock this year. Sales flop and ₹25 lakh piles up. The plan was ex ante; what happened is ex post.
points: Ex ante = planned or intended values; ex post = actual or realised values. They can differ.
Example: a firm plans inventory investment of ₹100 but sales fall short, so actual inventory investment becomes ₹130. Unplanned inventory accumulation = ₹30.
Aggregate demand (AD) = total planned expenditure on final goods and services: C + I + G + (X − M). In the two-sector model, AD = C + I.
Investment is the addition to the stock of physical capital (machines, buildings) and to inventories. In the simple model investment is autonomous: I = Ī (fixed, not dependent on income).
Income determination is based on ex ante (planned) values, because plans decide how much people want to buy.

example.q: A firm planned an inventory addition of ₹50 lakh. It produced goods worth ₹500 lakh, planned to sell ₹450 lakh, but sold only ₹420 lakh. Find ex post inventory investment and the unplanned part.
steps: Actual (ex post) inventory change = production − sales = 500 − 420 = 80

learn.reallife: Before Diwali, retailers in India plan large stocks (ex ante). Whether the festive season is strong decides the ex post stock left over in January.

topics.title: Consumption function, MPC and APC

learn.hook: Even a family with zero income must eat. That minimum spending, borrowed or from savings, is autonomous consumption.
points: Consumption function: C = C̄ + cY. C̄ is autonomous consumption (spending even at zero income); cY is induced consumption, which depends on income.
Marginal propensity to consume (MPC) c = ΔC / ΔY: the share of extra income spent on consumption. 0 < MPC < 1 (MPC = 0 or 1 are extreme limits).
Average propensity to consume (APC) = C / Y: the share of total income consumed.
At low income APC can be greater than 1 (consumption exceeds income because of C̄). APC falls as income rises.

example.q: Given C = 50 + 0.75Y, find C, APC and MPC when Y = 400.

learn.reallife: When the Centre cuts income tax, economists ask how much of the extra take-home pay Indian families will spend: that is the MPC.

Consumption rises with income, so 0 < MPC < 1.
APC can exceed 1 at very low incomes.
Autonomous consumption can make C larger than Y.
In C = C̄ + cY, c is the MPC.
It is the slope of the consumption function.
It is independent of income; induced consumption depends on income.
In C = 100 + 0.8Y, APC falls as income rises.
C̄/Y becomes smaller as Y grows.

topics.title: Saving function, MPS and APS

learn.hook: Every rupee of income has only two destinies in this model: you spend it or you save it. So MPC + MPS must equal one.
points: Saving = income − consumption. From C = C̄ + cY, the saving function is S = −C̄ + (1 − c)Y.
Marginal propensity to save (MPS) s = ΔS/ΔY = 1 − c. Average propensity to save (APS) = S/Y.
Since ΔC + ΔS = ΔY, MPC + MPS = 1. Since C + S = Y, APC + APS = 1.
At low incomes saving is negative (dissaving), so APS can be negative while APC exceeds 1.
Break-even income: the level of Y at which C = Y and S = 0. For C = C̄ + cY, it is Y = C̄/(1 − c).

example.q: Given C = 60 + 0.8Y, write the saving function and find S and APS at Y = 500. Also find the break-even income.

learn.reallife: Household saving is the biggest source of India's investment funds, which is why policy-makers watch the MPS closely.

topics.title: Equilibrium: AD = AS and S = I

learn.hook: If shoppers plan to buy more than factories produce, shelves empty. If they plan to buy less, warehouses fill. Equilibrium is where plans match output.
points: Aggregate supply (AS) is the total output (and income) Y in the economy. Equilibrium income is where planned AD = AS.
In the two-sector model AD = C̄ + Ī + cY = Ā + cY, where Ā = C̄ + Ī is autonomous expenditure. Equilibrium: Y = Ā + cY.
Saving-investment approach: equilibrium is where planned saving = planned investment (S = I).
If AD > output, inventories fall unexpectedly (unplanned decumulation) and firms raise output. If AD < output, inventories pile up (unplanned accumulation) and firms cut output.
With a government that taxes T, consumption depends on disposable income: C = C̄ + c(Y − T).

example.q: C̄ = 40, c = 0.8, Ī = 60. Output is 400. Is the economy in equilibrium? What will happen?
steps: Unplanned inventory fall of 20; firms raise output
example.answer: Not in equilibrium; output will rise towards 500

topics.title: Short-run equilibrium: the 45° line and algebra

learn.hook: Draw one 45° line and one AD line on a graph, and the point where they cross tells you the income of a whole nation. That's the Keynesian cross.
points: Short-run assumption: the price level is fixed. This is reasonable when there is unused capacity and unemployment, so firms can raise output without raising prices.
Graph (described in words): income Y on the horizontal axis, expenditure on the vertical axis. The 45° line from the origin shows all points where expenditure = income; it represents AS.
The consumption line starts at C̄ on the vertical axis with slope c. The investment line is horizontal at Ī. Adding them vertically gives the AD line, starting at Ā = C̄ + Ī with slope c.
Equilibrium is where the AD line cuts the 45° line. Algebra: Y = Ā + cY, so Y* = Ā / (1 − c) = (C̄ + Ī) / (1 − c).
To test whether a given income is in equilibrium, compare AD at that income with the income itself.

example.q: C̄ = 100, Ī = 50, c = 0.8. Find equilibrium income, and the consumption and saving at equilibrium.

learn.reallife: In 2020-21, idle capacity in Indian factories meant that more demand could raise output without much inflation, the fixed-price case Keynes described.

topics.title: Shifts of AD: autonomous and parametric

learn.hook: When the government announces a mega highway plan, the AD line jumps up. When people decide to spend a bigger share of every extra rupee, it tilts. Same graph, two very different moves.
points: A change in autonomous expenditure (C̄ or Ī) shifts the AD line parallel: up if Ā rises, down if it falls. The slope (c) does not change.
A parallel upward shift raises equilibrium income by more than the shift itself, through the multiplier.
A parametric shift is a change in a parameter of the function. A change in the MPC (c) changes the slope: the AD line swings (rotates) around its intercept Ā.
Higher c → steeper AD line → higher equilibrium income. Lower c → flatter AD line → lower equilibrium income.
A change in the intercept (C̄ or Ī) with the same c is also a parametric shift of the intercept, giving a parallel movement.

example.q: Ā = 100 and c rises from 0.75 to 0.8. Describe the AD shift and find the new equilibrium income.
steps: Change in c changes the slope: AD swings upward around Ā = 100
example.answer: AD becomes steeper; Y* rises from 400 to 500

topics.title: The investment multiplier

learn.hook: ₹100 crore spent on building a metro line becomes wages, which become spending at shops, which become more wages... The final rise in income can be several times ₹100 crore.
points: Investment multiplier k = ΔY / ΔI = 1 / (1 − MPC) = 1 / MPS.
Mechanism: an extra investment ΔI first raises income by ΔI. People spend c·ΔI, which becomes someone's income; they spend c²·ΔI, and so on.
Total ΔY = ΔI(1 + c + c² + c³ + ...) = ΔI / (1 − c), the sum of a geometric series with ratio c (0 < c < 1).
The larger the MPC (smaller the MPS), the larger the multiplier. Limits: k = 1 when MPC = 0; k → ∞ when MPC → 1.
ΔC = c·ΔY and ΔS = ΔI at the new equilibrium (saving rises to match the new investment).

example.q: MPC = 0.8 and investment rises by ₹100 crore. Find the multiplier, rise in income, rise in consumption and rise in saving.

topics.title: Effective demand, full employment and the paradox of thrift

learn.hook: Saving is good for a family. But if every family in India suddenly saves more, the nation's income could fall and total saving might not rise at all. Welcome to the paradox of thrift.
points: Full employment level of income: the output at which all who are willing and able to work at the prevailing wage are employed.
Involuntary unemployment: people willing to work at the going wage rate cannot find work.
Principle of effective demand: when prices are fixed, equilibrium output is decided by the level of AD. This equilibrium may be below full employment.
Paradox of thrift: if all people raise the proportion of income they save (MPS rises), total saving in the economy does not rise; it remains unchanged or falls, while income falls.
Reason: with investment autonomous, equilibrium needs S = Ī. A higher MPS lowers AD and income until total saving again equals the unchanged investment.

example.q: C̄ = 40, Ī = 60, MPC falls from 0.8 to 0.75 (MPS rises from 0.2 to 0.25). Show the paradox of thrift.
steps: Income falls by 100, total saving stays 60
example.answer: Income falls from 500 to 400; total saving unchanged at 60

learn.reallife: During uncertain times, if all households cut spending to save more, businesses from Surat textile units to Delhi restaurants may see sales fall, lowering incomes for everyone.

topics.title: Excess demand, deficient demand and their remedies

learn.hook: Too little demand empties factories; too much demand empties wallets through inflation. Policy-makers try to keep AD just right at full employment.
points: Deficient demand: AD is less than the AD needed for full-employment output. The shortfall at full employment is the deflationary gap. Effects: unsold stock, falling output and employment, possible fall in prices.

Excess demand: AD is more than the AD needed for full-employment output. The excess at full employment is the inflationary gap. Effects: prices rise without any rise in output, since resources are fully used.
Fiscal remedies: for deficient demand, raise government spending and cut taxes; for excess demand, cut government spending and raise taxes.
Monetary remedies: for deficient demand, lower repo/bank rate, CRR and SLR, buy securities, lower margins; for excess demand, do the opposite.

Graph in words: draw the AD line and the 45° line. At the full-employment output Y_F, the vertical gap between the 45° line and a lower AD line is the deflationary gap; the gap above it to a higher AD line is the inflationary gap.

example.q: Full-employment output is ₹1,000 crore. AD at full employment is ₹920 crore. Identify the situation and gap, and suggest one fiscal and one monetary measure.
steps: AD (920) < AS at full employment (1,000) → deficient demand
Fiscal: raise government spending; monetary: cut repo rate
example.answer: Deficient demand with a deflationary gap of ₹80 crore

chapters.title: Macroeconomics: Government Budget and the Economy

topics.title: The budget and the allocation function

learn.hook: Nobody sells tickets to street lights or national defence. If the market won't provide them, who will? Enter the government budget.
points: The government budget is an annual financial statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the government for a financial year (1 April to 31 March). Article 112 of the Constitution calls it the 'Annual Financial Statement'.
Allocation function: the government provides public goods that the market fails to supply in enough quantity, such as defence, roads, street lighting and public administration.
Public goods are non-rivalrous (one person's use does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (people who do not pay cannot easily be kept out).
Free-rider problem: since non-payers cannot be excluded, people avoid paying, so private firms cannot collect enough revenue. Hence the government provides public goods, financed by taxes.
Private goods (food, clothes, cars) are rivalrous and excludable and are supplied through markets.

example.q: Classify as public or private goods: (i) a lighthouse; (ii) a pizza; (iii) national defence; (iv) a seat in a cinema hall.
steps: Ask: is it non-rivalrous and non-excludable?
Lighthouse: ships cannot be kept from seeing it, and one ship's use doesn't reduce another's → public
Defence: protects everyone at once → public
Pizza and a cinema seat: one person's use excludes another's, and non-payers can be kept out → private

learn.reallife: Every February, the Union Finance Minister presents the Union Budget in Parliament, setting out how much will be spent on defence, railways, health and more.

topics.title: Redistribution, stabilisation and the two budget accounts

learn.hook: A tax on high incomes funding free school meals, and extra spending on highways during a slowdown: two different jobs done by the same budget.
points: Redistribution function: the government changes the distribution of income through taxes and transfers (pensions, subsidies, scholarships), so that disposable income is fairer.
Stabilisation function: the government uses its spending and taxes to reduce fluctuations in output and employment; raising AD in a slump and lowering it during inflation.
Other objectives: promoting economic growth (e.g. capital spending on infrastructure) and managing public enterprises.
The budget has two parts: the revenue budget (revenue receipts and revenue expenditure) and the capital budget (capital receipts and capital expenditure).
Fiscal policy means the use of government spending and taxation to achieve these objectives.

example.q: Identify the budget function: (i) old-age pensions for poor elderly; (ii) extra spending on roads in a recession; (iii) building a defence radar system.
steps: (i) a transfer to reduce inequality → redistribution
(ii) raising AD to fight a slump → stabilisation

topics.title: Revenue receipts: taxes and non-tax revenue

learn.hook: When you pay GST on a cricket bat and your parent pays income tax, both rupees land in the same place: the government's revenue receipts.
points: Revenue receipts are receipts that neither create a liability nor reduce an asset of the government. They are non-redeemable.
Tax revenue: direct taxes are paid by the person on whom they are imposed (personal income tax, corporation tax); indirect taxes can be shifted to others (GST, customs duties, excise duties).
Progressive taxation: tax rate rises as income rises. It reduces inequality and supports the redistribution function.

Non-tax revenue: interest on loans given by the government, dividends and profits from public sector undertakings, fees, fines, and grants received from foreign governments and international organisations.
GST (introduced on 1 July 2017) replaced many indirect taxes of the Centre and States.

topics.title: Revenue expenditure vs capital expenditure

learn.hook: Paying a teacher's salary keeps a school running this year. Building a new school building gives the country an asset for decades. The budget books them very differently.
points: Revenue expenditure neither creates assets nor reduces liabilities of the government: salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies, and grants to state governments (even if the grants are used for creating assets).
Capital expenditure either creates assets or reduces liabilities: building roads, dams and schools, buying machinery and land, buying shares, loans given to states and PSUs, and repayment of loans.
Interest payment on debt is revenue expenditure, but repayment of the loan principal is capital expenditure.
Capital expenditure raises the economy's productive capacity; revenue expenditure maintains the normal functioning of government.

example.q: Classify: (i) interest paid on public debt; (ii) repayment of a ₹1,000 crore loan; (iii) building a metro line; (iv) fertiliser subsidy.

topics.title: Capital receipts: debt and non-debt

learn.hook: When the government borrows ₹1 lakh crore, it gets cash today but owes it tomorrow. When it sells part of a PSU, it gets cash but owns less. Both are capital receipts.
points: Capital receipts either create a liability or reduce an asset of the government.

Debt-creating capital receipts: borrowings from the public (market loans), from the RBI and banks (treasury bills), loans from foreign governments and international bodies, and small savings such as post office deposits.
Non-debt-creating capital receipts: recovery of loans given earlier, and disinvestment proceeds (sale of shares in public sector undertakings).
Classification test: (1) Does it create a liability or reduce an asset? Then capital. (2) Neither? Then revenue.
Recovery of a loan is a capital receipt (reduces an asset), but interest on the loan is a revenue receipt.

example.q: Classify: (i) borrowing ₹500 crore from the market; (ii) ₹200 crore from selling shares of a PSU; (iii) ₹50 crore interest from states; (iv) ₹100 crore loan repaid by a state.
steps: (i) creates a liability → debt-creating capital receipt
(ii) reduces an asset → non-debt capital receipt
(iii) no liability, no asset reduction → revenue receipt
(iv) reduces an asset (the claim on the state) → non-debt capital receipt

topics.title: Revenue, fiscal and primary deficits

learn.hook: Each Budget Day, TV anchors quote one number above all: the fiscal deficit as a percentage of GDP. Here's how it is calculated.
points: Balanced budget: estimated receipts = expenditure. Surplus budget: receipts > expenditure. Deficit budget: expenditure > receipts.
Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts. It shows government dissaving: borrowing to meet current (consumption) needs.
Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt-creating capital receipts). It equals the government's total borrowing requirement.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments. It shows borrowing needed for current needs apart from paying interest on past debt.
Fiscal deficit can also be written as: revenue deficit + capital expenditure − non-debt capital receipts.

example.q: Revenue receipts = 800, revenue expenditure = 1,000, capital expenditure = 200, non-debt capital receipts = 50, interest payments = 150 (₹ crore). Find RD, FD and PD.

topics.title: Deficits, debt and the FRBM Act

learn.hook: Borrowing to pay interest on old borrowing is like using one credit card to pay another. Governments worry about this debt trap too.
points: Fiscal deficit is financed by borrowing (from the public, banks, abroad) or, in deficit financing, by borrowing from the RBI, which creates new money and can be inflationary.
High fiscal deficits raise public debt and future interest payments. Higher interest payments raise revenue expenditure and the revenue deficit, which can lead to a debt trap.
Heavy government borrowing can push up interest rates and crowd out private investment.
The revenue deficit is a part of the fiscal deficit: FD = RD + (capital expenditure − non-debt capital receipts). A high share of RD in FD means borrowing is used for consumption, not asset creation.

The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 set rules for fiscal discipline: reduce fiscal and revenue deficits over time (with a fiscal deficit target of 3% of GDP) and improve transparency.

topics.title: The open economy and the exchange rate

learn.hook: Your phone was assembled in Noida from parts made in Taiwan, paid for in rupees that were swapped for dollars. Welcome to the open economy.
points: An open economy interacts with other countries through three linkages: output markets (trade in goods and services), financial markets (buying and selling of financial assets) and labour markets (workers moving across countries).
Imports are a leakage from the domestic circular flow: spending goes to foreign producers. Exports are an injection: foreign spending on domestic output adds to AD.
The exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. In NCERT, e = rupees per unit of foreign currency, e.g. ₹83 per US dollar.
A rise in e means more rupees per dollar: the rupee has lost value. A fall in e means the rupee has gained value.
People accept a currency in international dealings only if they have confidence that it will keep its value.

example.q: The exchange rate moves from ₹80/$ to ₹84/$. A US tourist has $100. How many more rupees does she get, and what happened to the rupee?
steps: She gets ₹400 more; each dollar buys more rupees, so the rupee has lost value

topics.title: Balance of payments: the current account

learn.hook: India imports more goods than it exports, yet its current account deficit is much smaller than its trade deficit. The secret weapons: software exports and remittances.
points: Balance of payments (BoP): a systematic record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world during a year.

Current account records: trade in goods (visibles), trade in services, income flows (compensation of employees, investment income such as interest, profit and dividends) and transfer payments (gifts, remittances, grants).
Balance of trade (BoT) = exports of goods − imports of goods. A positive BoT is a trade surplus; negative is a trade deficit.
Net invisibles = net services (non-factor services like software, tourism, shipping, banking) + net income + net transfers.
Current account balance = balance of trade + net invisibles. Unlike BoT, it includes services, income and transfers.

topics.title: Current account deficit and the capital account

learn.hook: When a country spends more abroad than it earns, it must borrow or sell assets. The capital account shows exactly how.
points: Current account surplus: receipts exceed payments; the country is a net lender to the rest of the world. Current account deficit (CAD): the country is a net borrower.
Capital account records transactions in assets: foreign direct investment (FDI), foreign portfolio investment (FII/FPI), external commercial borrowings, and external assistance (aid loans).
Credit (inflow) entries: sale of domestic assets to foreigners and borrowing from abroad. Debit (outflow) entries: purchase of foreign assets and lending abroad.
Capital account surplus: inflows exceed outflows; deficit: outflows exceed inflows.
A CAD is not always alarming: if it finances investment that raises future exports and growth, it can be sustainable; if it finances consumption with short-term borrowing, it is risky.

example.q: Classify as capital account credit or debit for India: (i) a US firm sets up a factory in Pune; (ii) Tata buys a company in the UK; (iii) an Indian company borrows from a Japanese bank.
steps: (i) foreigners buy Indian assets → inflow → credit (FDI)
(ii) Indians buy foreign assets → outflow → debit
(iii) borrowing from abroad → inflow → credit (external borrowing)

topics.title: The BoP always balances: autonomous, accommodating and reserves

learn.hook: Accountants say the balance of payments always balances. Newspapers say India has a BoP surplus. Both are right. Here's how.
points: BoP identity: current account balance + capital account balance (including changes in official reserves) = 0. In this accounting sense the BoP always balances.

Autonomous transactions are undertaken for their own sake, e.g. profit, trade or investment (above the line). Accommodating transactions are made to cover the gap left by autonomous ones (below the line).

Official reserve transactions: the central bank selling or buying foreign exchange. BoP surplus = autonomous receipts exceed autonomous payments, and official reserves rise; BoP deficit = reserves fall.
Errors and omissions: a balancing item for transactions that could not be recorded correctly.

BPM6 (IMF's sixth manual) presents the BoP as a current account, a capital account (capital transfers, non-produced non-financial assets) and a financial account (FDI, portfolio investment, other investment and reserve assets).

example.q: Current account deficit = 40, capital account surplus (excluding reserves) = 55 ($ billion). What happens to official reserves? Is there a BoP surplus or deficit?
steps: A surplus of 15 is added to official reserves
BoP surplus of $15 billion; reserves rise by 15
example.answer: BoP surplus of $15 billion; reserves rise by $15 billion

learn.reallife: When the RBI's forex reserves climb to record levels, it usually means India's autonomous inflows exceeded autonomous outflows: a BoP surplus.

topics.title: The foreign exchange market: demand and supply

learn.hook: Every time an Indian student pays fees to a US university, someone in the forex market is buying dollars. Every time an Infosys client pays in dollars, someone is selling them.
points: The foreign exchange market is the market where national currencies are traded for one another. Participants: commercial banks, foreign exchange brokers, other authorised dealers and the central bank (RBI).
Demand for foreign exchange (say dollars) arises from: imports, travel and education abroad, gifts and remittances sent abroad, and purchase of foreign assets (investment abroad), plus speculation.
The demand curve for dollars slopes downward: when e (₹ per $) rises, imports become costlier in rupees, so fewer dollars are demanded.
Supply of foreign exchange comes from: exports, spending by foreign tourists, remittances from abroad, and foreign investment in India.
The supply curve slopes upward: when e rises, Indian goods become cheaper for foreigners, exports rise and more dollars are supplied.

example.q: At ₹80/$ a $500 US textbook costs an Indian student ₹40,000. At ₹85/$ what does it cost, and how does this explain the slope of the demand curve?
steps: The import is costlier in rupees
So fewer such imports (and dollars) are demanded at a higher e → downward slope
example.answer: ₹42,500; higher e reduces quantity of dollars demanded

learn.reallife: During the IPL season, foreign broadcasters' payments and tourists add to the supply of dollars, while Indian fans travelling abroad for the T20 World Cup add to the demand.
